content: Cow parsnip, scientifically referred to as Heracleum maximum (and also known as Indian celery or pushki), is the only species of the hogweed genus that is native to North America. Its taxonomic classification has been a subject of debate, with authoritative sources alternatively naming it Heracleum maximum, Heracleum lanatum, H. linatum, or categorizing it as a subspecies (H. sphondylium subsp. montanum) or a variety (H. sphondylium var. linatum) of the common hogweed (H. sphondylium). The classification used here aligns with the Integrated Taxonomic Information System (ITIS). This plant is distributed widely across North America, spanning from coast to coast. Within the continental United States, it is absent only in the southeastern states, from Texas eastward. In the western regions, it extends as far north as Alaska and is prevalent throughout most of Canada. Cow parsnip thrives at elevations up to 2,500 meters. While it is generally abundant and not considered a conservation concern, its population is declining in certain areas. For instance, it is listed as endangered in Kentucky, whereas in some western regions, it is regarded as an invasive weed. Cow parsnip is a tall herbaceous plant, often exceeding two meters in height. It features the characteristic flower umbels of the carrot family (Apiaceae), which are approximately 20 cm in diameter. These umbels may be flat-topped or more rounded in shape but are consistently white. The leaves are large, reaching up to 40 cm across, and are divided into lobes. The stems are robust and succulent. The plant's juices contain a phototoxin that, upon contact with the skin and subsequent exposure to ultraviolet light, can cause reactions ranging from mild rashes to severe blistering dermatitis, depending on individual sensitivity. This plant is considered a problematic weed, particularly in pastures, as it can taint the milk of cows that consume it. Historically, various Native American groups utilized cow parsnip extensively. All parts of the plant were employed for different purposes by one group or another. One of the most common uses was the preparation of poultices to treat bruises or sores. Additionally, the young stalks and leaf stems, harvested before the plant reached maturity, were consumed as food after peeling off the outer skin, which revealed a sweetish flavor. The dried stems were repurposed as drinking straws for the elderly or infirm and were also used to craft flutes for children. The roots of cow parsnip can be processed to produce a yellow dye. Furthermore, an infusion made from the flowers can be applied to the skin as a natural repellent against flies and mosquitoes.
